source.title: Derivative Manipulation for General Example Weighting.
source.authors: Xinshao Wang; E. Kodirov; Hua Yang; N. Robertson

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material provided; text is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper varies synthetic label-noise rates and reports training and test accuracies, bearing on V4. It does not test the original random-label intervention or the other versions’ stated outcomes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports experiments with partially corrupted labels, not completely random labels. It cites Arpit et al. for the claim that networks learn shared patterns before memorizing abnormal examples; that cited finding is not this paper’s result. Values in Table 10 report best and final test accuracy, corrupted-training-set accuracy, and intact-training-set accuracy. The supplementary figures show dynamics, but no precise values are extracted from them.
record.test_reason: The standard CCE baseline measures fitting and generalization across partial label-noise rates, bearing on V4. The clean Vehicles-10 regularization ablation also tests the clean-label generalization component of V5. DM's comparative performance does not itself test the standard-network claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that directly manipulating gradient magnitudes provides flexible example weighting and improves performance across their tasks; under increasing label noise, emphasizing relatively easier examples can improve robustness.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains models using derivative manipulation and compares accuracy under partial label corruption; it does not use the original random-label memorization experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise rate and the DM emphasis mode and variance affect reported training and test accuracies.

fits_no_version.finding: DM improves noisy-label test performance while deliberately reducing fitting to corrupted labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Example weighting can improve robustness by suppressing noisy-label fitting.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 2 and Section 4.1 report lower annotated-label probabilities for noisy examples and no noticeable increase for those examples under DM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Annotated-label probabilities distinguish clean and noisy examples during training; DM suppresses probability growth on noisy examples.

record.problems: No fully random-label condition. The reported CIFAR-10 results do not show perfect training accuracy; Table 10 reports selected settings and accuracy values rather than a complete sweep. Supplementary learning-dynamics figures have no extracted numeric values.
record.rows_left_out: Table 10 also reports best test accuracy and intact-training-set accuracy for each listed condition, plus additional DM emphasis modes. Omitted these separately reported measures and modes to prioritize corrupted-set fitting and final test accuracy within the row limit; see Supplementary Table 10. Other noisy-label experiments are outside the claim versions’ specific interventions.

untested.parts: No completely random labeling experiment or unchanged-hyperparameter demonstration of near-zero training error and chance test performance.
No random-versus-real-label training-time comparison or measured convergence slowdown across corruption rates.
No full sweep through completely random labels, and no demonstration that all corruption rates can reach perfect fit with sufficient training.
Random-label fitting with weight decay, dropout or augmentation is untested. The clean-label ablation covers L2 and dropout on Vehicles-10, not a separate removal of data augmentation.

The temporal ordering of learning real patterns and memorizing noise is not established by the supplied results. Clean/noisy label probabilities and endpoint subset accuracies do not establish that ordering.

missing.what: Clean-label regularization ablation: ResNet-44 on Vehicles-10 achieves 75.4% without regularization, 76.4% with L2, 77.9% with dropout and 78.7% with both.

Additional standard-CCE test-degradation results: CIFAR-100 ResNet-44 accuracy is 70.0%, 60.4%, 53.2% and 42.1% at symmetric noise rates 0%, 20%, 40% and 60%; CIFAR-10 GoogLeNet V1 accuracy is 85%, 74%, 74% and 35% at 0%, 20%, 40% and 80%. These test-only results show degradation but cannot establish perfect fitting.
missing.locator: Tables 1 and 2, Our Trained Results, CCE

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Symmetric corruption replaces labels uniformly among incorrect classes, rather than independently sampling from all classes. Endpoint training deficits qualify the observed training regime; they do not establish that these architectures cannot eventually memorize the data. Table 10 omissions explicitly declared in rows_left_out are not repeated as missing.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random labeling experiment; no test error at chance under fully random labels.
No comparison of training time for random versus true labels, or convergence slowdown across corruption rates.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiments.

The paper tests label-noise rates only through 80% on CIFAR-10 and 60% on CIFAR-100; it does not test all labels randomized. It reports accuracies rather than whether training error remains exactly zero at every rate. The reported results do not establish a steady rise in test error toward chance.
Regularizers are compared under 40% label noise, not random labels; removing regularization is not tested for its effect on generalization with true labels.
The paper cites the real-patterns-before-memorization finding but does not itself establish the temporal order of learning real versus random labels.
